questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: An ideological reading stated as a claim
questions.learningObjective: State an ideological reading as a claim that evidence could test.
questions.stem: A ticket asks the team to restate an ideological reading of a mural as a checkable claim. Which wording states the claim rather than assuming it?

options.text: The fresco presents labour as a moral virtue, which can be checked against its imagery.
The fresco was painted for a socialist government that funded all local murals.
options.misconception: assumes the funding source settles the patron's politics

options.text: The painter was a member of the same political party as the commissioner.
options.misconception: conflates the artist's politics with the patron's politics

options.text: The audience in 1938 read the mural as a celebration of the state.
options.misconception: treats one audience reaction as the work's fixed meaning

questions.explanation: An ideological reading must be stated so that evidence could confirm or unsettle it. Naming a patron's party or one audience's reaction adds facts the reading does not rest on.
questions.hint: Look for wording that evidence could confirm or unsettle.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reception history as a change of meaning
questions.learningObjective: Recognise reception history as a change of meaning across periods.
questions.stem: Another ticket lists three audience readings of the same relief with the years they were recorded. Which reading best shows reception as a change of meaning?

options.text: All three readings appear on one plaque dated 1804.
options.misconception: assumes one date explains every recorded reading

options.text: The panel was read as a warning in 1804, a tribute in 1902 and a motif in 1996.
The 1902 reading was entered in the artist's own diary.
options.misconception: credits the artist's diary as the audience's reception

options.text: The 1996 reading uses the same words as the 1804 reading.
options.misconception: treats a later citation as a repetition of the first

questions.explanation: Reception history tracks meaning shifting as audiences change. Three dated readings with different content show the work meaning different things, while a shared date removes that change.
questions.hint: Ask whether the readings differ across the dated entries.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reception after a relocation
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a relocation changes reception.
questions.stem: The drafting group asks what explains why a painting's reception changed after it was moved to a new building in 1968.

answer.exemplar: The move changed the viewing context, not the object itself. Displayed in a civic hall rather than a private collection, the painting met a broader public and was read through the new building's programme, so later accounts describe it differently from the earlier ones.

questions.explanation: A relocation changes who sees a work and its setting, and reception records reflect that context. Treating the change as a change in the object mistakes a new situation for a new artwork.
questions.hint: Separate what moved from what changed around it.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the criteria an attribution dossier leaves unaddressed.
questions.stem: A ticket lists nine criteria an attribution dossier must address. The review confirms six of them and marks one as not applicable. How many criteria remain unaddressed?
questions.explanation: Nine criteria minus the six confirmed leaves three, and one is marked not applicable, so nine minus six minus one equals two. Counting that item as confirmed would leave three instead.
questions.hint: Subtract both the confirmed and the not applicable counts.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why one document is not enough
questions.learningObjective: Judge the weight of a single document in an attribution.

stimulus.body: The team holds a single letter from 1911 written by the artist's dealer about a commission, in the artist's own hand. The rest of the dossier is empty. A reviewer wants to publish the attribution as settled.

questions.stem: A curator's note records that the team holds the single 1911 dealer letter. How far may the team rely on that one document?

options.text: Discard it entirely because a single source can never be accurate.
options.misconception: overcorrects by discarding evidence that can be corroborated

options.text: Treat it as decisive because it was written before the work was finished.
options.misconception: assumes the earliest document is the most reliable one

options.text: Treat it as one strand that still needs corroboration from independent evidence.
Treat it as decisive because dealers have no incentive to flatter.
options.misconception: assumes dealers never flatter, ignoring their own interest

questions.explanation: A single document may be accurate yet insufficient, since it can be miscopied or self-interested. It gains force when checked against independent evidence, so corroboration beats certainty.
questions.hint: Think about what a second, independent source would add.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What can revise an attribution
questions.learningObjective: Identify evidence that can revise an attribution.
questions.stem: The reviewers are asked to list what can revise an attribution and then to choose which example fits that description.

options.text: A newspaper review that called the work unusually polished.
options.misconception: mistakes a critic's praise for proof of the painter's hand

options.text: A later collector's opinion that the work lacks charm.
options.misconception: treats an aesthetic preference as evidence of authorship

options.text: A museum label written a decade after the attribution was published.
options.misconception: counts a later label as new evidence, not a repetition

options.text: A technical report showing a material the candidate painter never used.

questions.explanation: An attribution can be revised when evidence bears on the hand that made the object, such as materials the painter never used. Subjective charm and critical praise say nothing about authorship.
questions.hint: Ask which option touches the making of the object.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two independent lines revising a hand
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish two independent lines of evidence from one line repeated.
questions.stem: One proposal puts two separate findings together, both pointing away from a long-standing attribution. Which pairing counts as two independent lines?

options.text: Two critics who disagree about the quality of the brushwork.
options.misconception: counts two opinions of one feature as two separate lines

options.text: A pigment the painter never mixed, together with a canvas weave from a different mill.
A dated letter, together with the same letter quoted in a later book.
options.misconception: counts a quotation of one source as a second source

options.text: A restored passage, together with the varnish laid over that passage.
options.misconception: counts one treatment and its overlying layer as two lines

questions.explanation: Two independent lines come from different kinds of evidence, each able to stand alone. Two opinions of brushwork are one line, a repeated quotation is one source, varnish over repair is one treatment.
questions.hint: Ask whether each finding could survive without the other.

questions.topic: What connoisseurship vocabulary grades

questions.stem: A dealer's grading of a drawing reads fine, well preserved, attributed and in good state. What does this vocabulary actually grade?

options.text: The object's market price against comparable works sold last year.
options.misconception: reads a connoisseur's adjectives as a market valuation

options.text: How certain the dealer is that the named artist made the piece.
options.misconception: assumes quality words carry a claim about the artist's hand

options.text: Quality and preservation as the dealer sees them, not who made the object.
How much the object should be insured for at its next sale.
options.misconception: reads descriptive grading terms as a financial appraisal

questions.explanation: Terms like fine or well preserved grade quality and condition, a dealer's assessment of the object. They judge degree, not who made the work, which must be argued from separate evidence.
questions.hint: Separate judgements of quality from claims of authorship.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: An ideological reading stated as a claim
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish an ideological claim from a political verdict.
questions.stem: The curators ask what separates an ideological reading stated as a claim from a political verdict passed on the same tapestry.

answer.exemplar: A claim states what the work asserts and how, and names the evidence that could confirm or unsettle it, so a reader can weigh it against the object itself. A verdict judges the work or its maker as good or bad, closing the question rather than opening an argument that evidence can test.

questions.explanation: A claim states what the work asserts and names evidence that could test it. A verdict approves or condemns outside evidence, so a tested reading stays arguable while judgement closes it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the statement could be proved wrong.

questions.hint: Divide the devotional count by all twenty-four accounts.

questions.topic: Reception after a relocation
questions.learningObjective: Read a change of reception against a change of setting.

stimulus.body: In 1974 the tapestry moved from a private school to the city museum, which displayed it beside maps of the region. Visitors' books from 1975 describe it as a patriotic allegory, while school labels from 1958 call it a temperance scene.

options.text: The tapestry was physically altered during the move to match the maps.
options.misconception: confuses a change of surroundings with a change of object

options.text: The school labels were written by a later owner who disliked temperance.
options.misconception: blames one hostile owner instead of the display context

options.text: Visitors in 1975 were paid to describe the tapestry in patriotic terms.
options.misconception: invents a payment that the visitor books do not record

options.text: The new setting let viewers read the tapestry against the maps beside it.

questions.explanation: The reception changed because the setting changed, and the visitor books reflect that context. Claims about a hostile owner, paid visitors or physical alteration appear nowhere in the records.
questions.hint: Consider what the new display placed next to the work.

The fact that the work hangs in a gallery devoted to the proposed painter.
options.misconception: confuses where a work hangs with evidence about its maker

options.text: A long list of similar-looking works sharing the candidate's nickname.
options.misconception: treats resemblance to a nickname as documented practice

questions.explanation: An attribution rests on evidence about the making of the object, compared with what is documented for the candidate. Praise, current location and resemblance to a nickname contribute no such evidence.
questions.hint: Look for the option about materials or technique.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the limits of a single document for an attribution.
questions.stem: A single signed receipt for a painting is held up in a ticket as proof of who painted it. What should the team say?

options.text: The receipt is worthless, since dealers write receipts for anything.
options.misconception: overstates the doubt and discards usable evidence

options.text: The receipt settles authorship, since a signature implies the artist's hand.
options.misconception: reads a receipt signature as a signature on the painting

options.text: The receipt supports a purchase, and authorship still needs other evidence.
The receipt settles authorship, since buyers choose known artists only.
options.misconception: assumes buyers only purchase works they can attribute

questions.explanation: A receipt documents a transaction and may name a seller, not the painter. It supports the object's history, but authorship still needs evidence about how the work was made.
questions.hint: Ask what a receipt actually witnesses.

questions.topic: What can revise an attribution
questions.learningObjective: Choose which development can revise an attribution.
questions.stem: Four developments are listed in a museum's holding of a painting, and one of them could revise the 1912 attribution. Which one is it?

options.text: A 2010 loan request describing the work as a prized example of the school.
options.misconception: treats an owner's enthusiasm as a finding about authorship

options.text: A 1970 exhibition that displayed the work beside works of the same school.
options.misconception: treats a juxtaposition of related works as evidence

options.text: A 2001 catalogue entry that repeats the 1912 attribution without comment.
options.misconception: counts a repeated attribution as though it were new analysis

options.text: A 1998 report finding a modern synthetic binder in the ground layer.

questions.explanation: A revision needs evidence about how the object was made. A synthetic binder in the ground layer points away from the proposed painter's materials, while exhibitions and catalogue entries restate it.
questions.hint: Ask which development bears on the materials.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two independent lines revising a hand
questions.learningObjective: Explain why independent lines outweigh repeated opinions.
questions.stem: Two independent findings are said to overturn a long-standing attribution while two agreeing opinions cannot. Explain the difference.

answer.exemplar: Each independent finding comes from a different kind of evidence, so one cannot simply repeat the other, and each can be checked and sustained on its own; two opinions, however agreeing, share the same basis and therefore add weight of agreement rather than weight of evidence.

questions.explanation: Evidence gains force by being independent, so one line cannot carry another's errors; two agreeing opinions repeat a single line. Independence of kind, not number of voices, moves an attribution.
questions.hint: Count the kinds of evidence, not the number of voices.

options.misconception: states a motive for the commission without evidence

Viewers in the town always read the mural as a political statement.

questions.topic: Reception history as a change of meaning
questions.learningObjective: Define reception history and distinguish it from related enquiries.

options.misconception: reduces reception history to a list of owners and dealers

options.text: Reception history records the single meaning the artist intended in 1600.
options.misconception: confuses reception history with recovering intention

options.text: Reception history tracks how meanings change across periods and audiences.
Reception history ranks how well later viewers understood the original.
options.misconception: turns reception history into a ranking of viewers

questions.explanation: Reception history follows how a work is interpreted at different times and by different viewers, so meaning changes. Intent, ownership and judging viewers are other kinds of study.
questions.hint: Ask whether meaning is treated as fixed or changing.

options.misconception: replaces a question about audiences with one about money

options.misconception: assumes a change of setting leaves the readings unchanged

options.misconception: describes the transport rather than the reception after

options.text: The new setting and the audiences it brought, and how descriptions changed.

questions.topic: What an attribution rests on
questions.learningObjective: Assess what an attribution dossier actually establishes.
questions.stem: A dossier's contents are described in one ticket. What does the dossier actually establish about the attribution?

options.text: The work shares the candidate's materials, which settles the attribution completely.
options.misconception: turns supporting evidence into proof and overstates it

options.text: The work shares the candidate's materials and preparation, which supports it without proving it.

options.misconception: mistakes resemblance in style for technical agreement

options.misconception: treats a recent cleaning as if it revealed new facts

questions.explanation: Shared materials and preparation bear on the hand, so they support an attribution without closing the question. Style alone and a recent cleaning add nothing to what was actually observed.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why one document is not enough
questions.learningObjective: Explain why one document cannot close an attribution.
questions.stem: One document is asked to explain why it can never settle an attribution, and what would make such a document count for more.

answer.exemplar: A single document records one act by one person at one moment, so it can be miscopied, mistaken or self-serving, and it cannot be checked against anything else. It gains weight when it is supported by an independent line of evidence, such as technical analysis or a documented provenance.

questions.explanation: One document has a single source, so its errors go unchecked and it may reflect its writer's interests. Its weight grows when an independent line of evidence supports the same conclusion.
questions.hint: Ask what independent check the document allows.

options.text: Publish it as settled, since an undated photograph is the oldest source.
options.misconception: treats the age of a source as a guarantee of its accuracy

options.text: Publish it as settled, since photographs do not distort the evidence.
options.misconception: assumes photographs cannot distort or misidentify an object

options.misconception: discards a usable source because a copy is unavailable

options.text: Publish the attribution as provisional, pending an independent line of evidence.

questions.explanation: One undated photograph is a single source with no check on it, so it supports a provisional attribution, not a settled one. Withdrawal wastes evidence, and age says nothing about accuracy.
questions.hint: Ask how many independent sources the file holds.

options.misconception: counts a preference for a name as evidence about the maker

questions.topic: What an attribution rests on
questions.learningObjective: State what an attribution rests on.
questions.stem: A final ticket asks the group first to state what an attribution rests on and then to choose the option that fits.

options.text: The smoothness of the surface, which no imitator has matched since.
options.misconception: rests on a general impression of the surface, not analysis

options.text: The consistency of the attribution across catalogues published since 1900.
options.misconception: treats repeated publication as evidence about the maker

options.text: The reputation of the scholar who first proposed the name in 1911.
options.misconception: measures the attribution by the standing of its proposer

options.text: A correspondence of materials, technique and handling with documented practice.

questions.explanation: An attribution rests on comparison with the candidate's documented practice. Agreement between catalogues, the proposer's reputation and an impression of the surface add no evidential weight.
questions.hint: Ask what the comparison must be with.
